title: Stephen (Acts 6:8–7:60)
hook: the first to die for the faith forgives his killers as the stones fall
carry: lay not this sin to their charge

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Beautiful Gate: no silver or gold, just a hand up, and a man leaping.
screen: `SUCH AS I HAVE, GIVE I THEE.`

segments.voice: An argument breaks out in Jerusalem: some widows are being left out of the daily food. The apostles ask the believers to choose seven people to run the tables. The first name on the list is Stephen, a man, Acts says, full of faith and of the Holy Spirit. A food organizer, but also a speaker, he gets into fierce debates in a Jerusalem synagogue, all of them Jews, arguing about Jesus, the temple and the law. It ends with Stephen hauled before the council, where witnesses Acts calls false swear he's been speaking against the holy place. Everyone in the room looks at him, and Luke says they saw his face as it had been the face of an angel.
screen: `SEVEN TO RUN THE TABLES.` → `A FIERCE DEBATE.` → `THE FACE OF AN ANGEL.`

segments.voice: Stephen answers with a long speech: the history of his people, from Abraham to Moses to the temple, and in it God keeps meeting them far from any temple, in Mesopotamia, in Egypt, in the wilderness. By the end the room is furious. Stephen looks up and says he sees heaven opened, and Jesus standing at God's right hand. They cover their ears, drag him outside the city, and stone him. While the stones fall, he prays two things. "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." Then, kneeling, loudly: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." Sound familiar? On the cross, in Luke's Gospel, Jesus prays, "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do," and then commits his spirit into his Father's hands. Luke tells Stephen's death as an echo of his teacher's. Martyr comes from the Greek martys, which first meant simply a witness, someone who tells a court what they saw. Stephen is remembered as the first Christian martyr, and over time the word changed, until it meant a witness who dies rather than take back what they saw. To be clear: this was a bitter quarrel among Jews, Stephen and the believers around him included, not a story about one people against another. And a quiet detail at the edge of the scene: the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. Hold on to that name. Church tradition keeps Stephen's feast just after Christmas.
screen: `A HISTORY, TOLD TO THE COUNCIL.` · `LORD JESUS, RECEIVE MY SPIRIT.` · `MARTYS: A WITNESS.` · `COATS AT THE FEET OF SAUL.` · then, large: `LAY NOT THIS SIN TO THEIR CHARGE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has hurt you, not the biggest wound, one you can hold for two minutes. You don't have to tell them or say it was fine; Stephen didn't, he asked that it not be held against them, so see if you can let go of the charge, even a little. If you pray, use his words; if not, just loosen your grip.
Martyr. From the Greek martys, a witness. Stephen, remembered as the first, who forgave as he died.
Your line: lay not this sin to their charge. Tomorrow, a chariot on a desert road. Day seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Christians honor Stephen as the first martyr, with a feast day on December 26 in Western churches and December 27 in many Orthodox churches. His dying prayer of forgiveness is often read alongside Jesus's words from the cross.

original.note: Greek: a witness, someone who testifies to what they saw. Later, one who dies for that witness.

trapdoor: what you thought: a martyr is someone who dies for a cause.
what it means: Stephen is a witness who won't unsay what he saw, and who forgives the people killing him.
what a scholar hears: martys was a courtroom word; Luke shapes Stephen's death to echo Jesus's, and slips in Saul, holding the coats, to set up the next turn of Acts.

notes: History framing: the script stresses that this was a dispute among Jews (Acts 6:9 names synagogue members from several places) and not one people against another. Confirm tone.
Luke 23:34 is missing from some early manuscripts; not mentioned in the script.
Feast days: December 26 (Western); December 27 in Orthodox churches on the Byzantine calendar. Confirm.
The development of martys from 'witness' to 'one who dies' is summarized as happening over the following centuries; confirm phrasing.
